newsitem.title: USA: Fujimori, rebels clash over Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori, rebels clash over Peru crisis.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, on a private visit to the United States, on Sunday walked right back into a deadlock with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.

Fujimori, who earlier spoke optimistically about the group "implicitly" dropping its main demand for the release of jailed comrades, was quickly corrected by the international spokesman for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.

"There is nothing implicit. Fujimori is misinterpreting what we have said from the beginning that our global proposal is negotiable," MRTA spokesman Isaac Velazco told Reuters in a telephone interview from Hamburg.
Later, a top Peruvian official travelling with Fujimori played down the controversy over the president's comments about the guerrillas' negotiating position.
"What is happening now is normal in a negotiating process," Victor Joy Way, the speaker of Peru's House of Deputies, told Reuters.
"There will be ups and downs, comings and goings but I think that rationality will prevail," he added.
However, Joy Way insisted on the point that the Peruvian government will not negotiate the freedom of guerrillas who have already been sentenced and jailed.
Fujimori arrived in Washington on Saturday from Toronto, where he held an emergency summit with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

The two leaders agreed to push for direct talks with the rebels, who have held the Japanese residence since Dec. 17., but ruled out the guerrillas' demand for the liberation of about 400 MRTA members jailed in Peru.
Fujimori put a positive spin on the situation in interviews on Saturday, when he said he was optimistic about talks because the rebels had "implicitly" given ground on their main demand.
"We convinced them they can't push the liberation of MRTA prisoners; it took a lot of time, but we were very patient," Fujimori said in the interview with The Washington Post.
Velazco said, however, that the MRTA was sticking to its bargaining position "100 percent" -- although he did hint that talks on other issues might go forward.

Along with freedom for their comrades, the rebels have also demanded improved prison conditions, an overhaul of Peru's secret court system for people accused of terrorism and an end to Fujimori's free-market economic reforms.

"In negotiation there have to be concessions. We are not trying to impose on the government but nor do we want the government to impose on us," Velazco said. "We have to arrive at points that satisfy both sides."

The leader of the MRTA, who is one of about 15 heavily-armed guerrillas holding the mansion in an upscale Lima neighbourhood, reiterated on Sunday that any government move to force them out would end in tragedy.

"We know (an assault by the Peruvian army) would be tragic for the gentlemen held captive here. We are sorry for them and for their families," Nestor Cerpa Cartolino said in an interview with two Spanish newspapers.
"We are not afraid. If they decide to use force, they will find every one of us prepared for combat. We are aware that if things turn out this way, we will not leave alive."
Before returning to Lima on Monday, Fujimori is scheduled to meet with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and other State Department officials to discuss the crisis.
The rebels originally took more than 500 hostages during a lavish cocktail party at the diplomatic mansion but have freed most of them.
The remaining 72 captives in the mined and booby-trapped residence include two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and Fujimori's brother.
